findings.description: scheduleTask now reads `handleOrId.refresh` for any non-number return value. Some polyfills and environments return `undefined` or `null` from setTimeout/setInterval/setImmediate/requestAnimationFrame, and the old code explicitly guarded against this. In that case `isFunction(handleOrId.refresh)` throws a TypeError while scheduling the task, which is a regression for those environments.

If the native setTimeout/setInterval/setImmediate/requestAnimationFrame returns a non-number that is also undefined or null (the removed comment said some polyfills and browsers do this), the new `else` branch evaluates `handleOrId.refresh` and throws a TypeError. Previously this case was tolerated: `handleId` was just set to undefined and the task was returned.

The block that set `task.ref` and `task.unref` (bound to the Node handle) was removed. Any code that calls `ref()` or `unref()` on the returned task, which is what callers receive when no handle is returned, now fails because those methods no longer exist. This is a silent behavior regression.

`_pseudoFunctionAwareScopeSelectorPart` assumes any part starting with `:is(` or `:where(` ends with the closing `)`, and does `selectorPart.slice(prefix.length, -1)`. Parts are only split on top-level combinators, so a part like `:is(.a):hover`, `:where(.a).b` or `:is(h1, h2)::before` has trailing text after the paren. The slice then drops the last character of that trailing text instead of the paren. The result is garbled CSS, e.g. `:is(.a):hover` becomes `:is(.a)[contenta]:hove)`. The test for `:where(a):where(b)` only matches because of an odd expected output; that case is broken in the same way.

The new `ts_test_library` and `karma_web_test_suite` targets are appended, but the diff adds no `load(...)` statements for them in this file. The sibling `ng-debug-api/BUILD.bazel` does add them. If this file does not already load them, Bazel analysis of the package fails with an undefined-symbol error, which breaks every target in the package.

The new `sortedProviders` computed was added to apply the old sort-by-token behavior, but the template still passes the raw `providers()` input to `<ng-injector-providers>`. Providers are now unsorted, and the sorting that previously happened in the message handler is lost.

`init()` is called inside the `afterRenderEffect` write phase, which reruns whenever `componentExplorerView` changes. Each run registers another `highlightComponent` listener on the message bus, so the listeners accumulate and fire multiple times. Each run also recreates both tree visualizers via `setUpEnvironmentInjectorVisualizer` and `setUpElementInjectorVisualizer`. Zoom and pan state is lost on every view update, and `injectorTreeGraph` and `elementInjectorTreeGraph` are rebuilt every time.

`diDebugAPIsAvailable` is now computed from the latest view only. A view with an empty forest, or one without `resolutionPath`, flips it to false. The `@else` branch then destroys the whole wrapper and its visualizers, and the 'not supported' message shows. Previously the flag stayed true once set. Before the first view arrives, `componentExplorerView` is null, so the 'only available on Angular 17+' message flashes incorrectly.

The `.hidden` class CSS (display:none) was replaced with the `[hidden]` attribute on component host elements. The UA rule `[hidden]{display:none}` is overridden by any author `display` style on the hosts (for example `display:block` or flex). If the hosts set `display`, the inactive tabs would remain visible and overlap the active tab. The injector tree's special visibility workaround was also removed.

The afterRenderEffect write callback calls `this.init()` every time `componentExplorerView` changes. Each call registers another `highlightComponent` listener on the message bus, so listeners leak and duplicate. Each call also recreates both InjectorTreeVisualizers through `setUpEnvironmentInjectorVisualizer` and `setUpElementInjectorVisualizer`, which discards zoom and pan state and the existing graph on every explorer view update. Previously this setup ran once.

The template still passes `providers()` (the raw input) to `ng-injector-providers`. The new `sortedProviders` computed is never used. The providers list used to be sorted by token in the message handler, so the sorting is now silently lost and providers appear in arbitrary order.

Tab visibility now relies on the native `hidden` attribute on custom elements, replacing the removed `.hidden {display:none}` class. The child components' `:host` styles set `display` (block or flex), and author styles override the user-agent `[hidden]{display:none}` rule. The inactive tabs may therefore stay visible and stack on top of each other. The removed special case for the injector tree (visibility:hidden, so the SVG keeps its layout dimensions) also means the graph may now render with zero size while the tab is hidden.

The devapp now packages zone.js from `//:node_modules/zone.js`, so it is served under `node_modules/zone.js/...` instead of `npm/node_modules/zone.js/...`. The matching `index.html` for this app (and the shell-browser `index.html`) is not updated in this diff, unlike the demo-standalone one. If either still has `<script src="./npm/node_modules/zone.js/bundles/zone.umd.min.js">`, the zone.js script will 404 and the app will fail to bootstrap. The removal of `tslib.js` from the package could also break the app if anything still loads it.

The zone.js dependency moved from the `@npm//:node_modules/zone.js/bundles/zone.umd.min.js` file to the `//:node_modules/zone.js` package target. That changes where the file lands in the pkg_web output: it moves from `npm/node_modules/zone.js/...` to `node_modules/zone.js/...`. Only demo-standalone's index.html was updated to the new path. The other HTML pages (devtools/src/index.html and shell-browser's index.html) were not changed, so if they still use `./npm/node_modules/zone.js/bundles/zone.umd.min.js`, zone.js will 404 and the apps will fail to load. The same applies to the shell-browser filegroup.

lookup_field now returns the final related field as `f` for any `__` path. `items_for_result` treats a non-None, non-auto_created `f` as a field on the result row itself. If the path ends in a ForeignKey (e.g. `parent__parent`), `f.remote_field` is a ManyToOneRel, so the code runs `getattr(result, f.name)` on the wrong model. The result is either an AttributeError or the wrong object displayed. Before this change `f` was None for these paths, so the value was rendered correctly. Separately, `get_fields_from_path` is called unguarded and can raise FieldDoesNotExist or NotRelationField for paths that resolve through `getattr` but are not pure field paths. Those columns would crash the changelist instead of rendering.

`get_fields_from_path(opts.model, name)` is called whenever `name` contains `__` and the attribute walk succeeded. The walk uses plain `getattr`, so it succeeds for properties, methods or other non-field attributes on related objects (e.g. `parent__some_property`). In that case `get_fields_from_path` raises `FieldDoesNotExist` or `NotRelationField`, which is not caught. This turns a lookup that used to return a value (changelist and readonly fields) into an exception, a regression for existing users.

`f` is now a real field for related paths, so `items_for_result` takes its `else` branch. If the final field is a ForeignKey (`isinstance(f.remote_field, ManyToOneRel)`), that branch runs `getattr(result, f.name)`. Here `f.name` belongs to the related model, not the row's model, so it raises AttributeError or returns the wrong object for `list_display` entries like `parent__parent`. Previously these rendered the value correctly with `f=None`.

Validation relies on `validate_field.formfield().to_python(bit)`, but for fields with `choices` the form field is a TypedChoiceField. Its `to_python` only returns a string and does not validate or coerce it. For example, with an IntegerField that has choices and `search_fields=['status__exact']`, searching for 'foo' passes validation unchanged. The ORM then calls `int('foo')` in `get_prep_value`, which raises ValueError and causes a 500 error. The removed Cast-based code handled this case, so this is a regression. Related: for ForeignKey/relation fields `ModelChoiceField.to_python` runs an extra DB query per search term and returns a model instance.

Validation relies on `formfield().to_python()`, which does not validate the type for every field. A non-text field with `choices` (for example an IntegerField) gets a TypedChoiceField. Its `to_python()` only returns `str(value)` and does no coercion or choice check, because coercion happens in `clean()`. A term like 'foo' therefore passes validation and is used in `int_field__exact='foo'`. That raises `ValueError: Field 'x' expected a number` and the changelist crashes with a 500. The removed Cast approach did not crash here.

For ForeignKey exact lookups (such as `author__exact`), `formfield()` returns a ModelChoiceField. Its `to_python()` runs a database query for every search term and every such field. It also applies `limit_choices_to` and the field's queryset, so a term that matches an existing row can be silently dropped. Instantiating the formfield for every term is extra overhead. An empty quoted term (`""`) is converted to None by many formfields, and `exact=None` is then turned into an IS NULL lookup, which changes the meaning of the search.

The new wrap() drops blank lines and trailing newlines. For an empty or whitespace-only line, `wrapper.wrap(line)` returns `[]`, so nothing is appended. Paragraph breaks such as "a

b" therefore collapse to "a
b". A trailing newline is also lost, because `"
".join(...)` adds no final newline and TextWrapper drops trailing whitespace. The old implementation preserved both, so `wordwrap` output changes for existing users. It also removes intentional indentation and whitespace-only lines.

The rewrite using textwrap.TextWrapper with the default drop_whitespace and replace_whitespace changes behavior. Each line from splitlines(True) is wrapped separately, and wrapper.wrap() returns [] for blank or whitespace-only lines such as "
". Blank lines and paragraph breaks are therefore dropped. Trailing newlines are also lost because the result is joined with "
". Leading and intermediate whitespace (indentation, multiple spaces) is stripped or collapsed as well. For example, wrap("a

b", 10) now gives "a
b" instead of preserving the blank line. This is a regression for existing users of the wordwrap filter and wrap().

The check `".." in str(filter_expression.var)` is too broad. For a constant (a quoted string literal or a number), `FilterExpression.var` is the resolved value rather than a `Variable`. So `{{ "Wait..." }}` or `{{ "a..b" }}` is not a lookup at all, yet it triggers the double-dot deprecation warning. When the deprecation ends and the commented-out error is enabled, valid templates with literal strings containing `..` such as ellipses would raise `TemplateSyntaxError`. For `Variable` objects, `str()` returns the repr, which relies on incidental formatting. The check should apply only when `var` is a `Variable` that does lookups, and should inspect `var.var`.

The check `".." in str(filter_expression.var)` also matches string literals, not just variable lookups. For `{{ "Loading..." }}` or `{{ "a..b" }}`, `FilterExpression.var` is the resolved literal string, which contains `..`. This emits a spurious RemovedInDjango70Warning for valid templates. Once the deprecation ends and the warning becomes an error, those templates would raise TemplateSyntaxError. The check should only apply to real variable lookups, for example when `var` is a `Variable` with `lookups` and not a literal.

The prefetch filter now builds ColPairs with `queryset.model._meta.db_table` as the alias, for every forward FK including single-column ones. If the target field is defined on a parent model (multi-table inheritance, or a `to_field` inherited from a parent), its column lives in the parent's table, not the child's. The generated SQL then references a column that does not exist on the child table, with no join to the parent, so the prefetch fails. It also bypasses normal alias resolution for aliased or joined querysets and for custom querysets with `select_related`. The previous name-based `filter(<field>__in=...)` resolved joins correctly, so this is a regression for existing users.

`writer="html"` passes a string to the `writer` argument of `docutils.core.publish_parts`. Before docutils 0.22, that argument expects a Writer instance and string names go through `writer_name`. The Publisher would then keep the string as `self.writer` and fail with an AttributeError when it reads writer attributes such as `settings_spec`. That would break all admindocs RST rendering on older docutils versions that Django still supports. Nothing in the diff guards against this or raises the minimum docutils version.

`writer` was documented as a Writer instance until docutils 0.22 added support for a component name string. On older docutils, `writer="html"` is stored as the writer object, so `publish_parts` likely fails with an AttributeError because a str has no `write` method. `writer_name` was the supported way to pass a name there, so admindocs RST rendering would break on docutils releases before 0.22 unless the code is version-gated or the minimum docutils version is raised.

The new <button> elements are created without type="button", so they default to type="submit" inside the admin form. Their only protection against submitting the form is e.preventDefault() in the click handlers. Any activation path that bypasses those handlers, or a handler that throws before reaching preventDefault, will submit the form. The old <a href="#"> links had no such risk.

The search-label help icons had their `title` attribute replaced by `aria-label` on an empty <span> with no role. Sighted users lose the hover tooltip, and most screen readers ignore aria-label on a generic span, so the help text is no longer reachable by anyone.

The database-feature warnings (W037, W040, W043) scan all of `model._meta.indexes` via `any(... for index in model._meta.indexes)`, and the W037 test even uses `self.condition` inside the generator. `Index.check()` now runs once per index, so each of these warnings is emitted once per index in the model whenever any index triggers it. Previously there was one warning per model per database. A model with several indexes will report duplicate warnings.

The field check uses `self.fields`, which keeps the '-' prefix on descending fields (e.g. '-name'). The old code used `fields_orders`, which strips the prefix. For `Index(fields=['-name'])`, `_check_local_fields` now looks up the field '-name' and reports a bogus E012 nonexistent-field error, a regression for valid descending indexes.

All index checks now run only inside the `for db in databases` loop and only when `allow_migrate_model` is true. When `Model.check()` is called without `databases`, or the router disallows the model on every database, the name checks (E033/E034) and field-reference checks (E012/E013/E016 and similar) are silently skipped. They previously ran unconditionally, so this is a regression, and the test changes that add `databases=self.databases` hide it. With several databases the same name and field errors are also reported once per database.

The field check now uses `self.fields`, which keeps the '-' prefix on descending fields (e.g. `fields=['-name']`). The old code used `fields_orders`, which strips the prefix. `_check_local_fields` will now report a nonexistent field '-name' for valid descending indexes, a false E012-style error. Passing a set also makes the order of reported errors nondeterministic.

The feature checks iterate over `model._meta.indexes` instead of testing this index. The W037 check uses `self.condition` inside a generator over `index`, and the W040 and W043 checks use `index.include` and `index.contains_expressions` across all indexes. A model with N indexes where one has a condition, include or expression gets that warning N times, and indexes that don't use the feature emit it too. Each check should test only `self`.

Index name and field checks (E033, E034, nonexistent, m2m and non-local field errors) now run only inside the per-database loop. They are skipped when `databases` is empty or None, and when `router.allow_migrate_model` is False for every database. Previously they ran unconditionally. With several databases, the same errors are reported once per database, so they are duplicated.

`relatedWindows` is declared as a block-scoped `const relatedWindows = []` inside the file's `{ ... }` block, so it is not a property of `window`. Changing the references to `window.relatedWindows` makes `window.relatedWindows` undefined in production. `dismissRelatedLookupPopup` then throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'indexOf')` after setting the value and before `win.close()`. The raw-id lookup popup would never close. The new test hides this by assigning `window.relatedWindows` in `beforeEach`.

`relatedWindows` is a local `const` inside the file's IIFE and is never exposed on `window`. Changing the references to `window.relatedWindows` makes `window.relatedWindows` undefined in production, so `.indexOf` throws a TypeError. That happens right after the value is set and before `win.close()`, so the raw-id lookup popup never closes and is never removed from the tracked windows. The new tests hide this by assigning `window.relatedWindows = []` in `beforeEach`. The code should keep using the closure variable.

The PR title and description say `dismissRelatedLookupPopup` should trigger a `change` event after setting the value (ticket #31170). The diff only swaps `document.getElementById(name).value` for `elem.value`, with no `change` event trigger. Dependent fields are therefore still not updated, and the stated fix is missing.

In the insert path, an expression-valued field is appended to returning_fields without checking whether it is already there. `meta.db_returning_fields` includes fields with a `db_default`. If such a field is assigned an expression such as `Now()` or `F()`, it is added twice, so the SQL becomes `RETURNING col, col`. This is redundant and can fail on backends such as Oracle, where RETURNING ... INTO needs distinct binds. The guard `if field not in returning_fields` is missing.

In the insert path, a field whose value is an expression is appended to returning_fields unconditionally. A field with a db_default is already in meta.db_returning_fields. If it is assigned an expression such as F() or Now(), it gets added a second time, so the RETURNING clause lists the same column twice. Backends may reject or mishandle duplicate columns, for example Oracle's RETURNING ... INTO. The fix is to append only if the field is not already in returning_fields.

get_supported_language_variant() now raises ValueError for over-long codes (when strict, or when no '-' fallback exists). Existing callers only catch LookupError. get_language_from_path() passes the regex-matched first URL path segment, e.g. '/xxxx…(>500 chars)/', so LocaleMiddleware and i18n_patterns can crash with an unhandled ValueError (HTTP 500) on a long URL segment. The get_language_from_request() paths that use the cookie or header values have the same problem. Previously these inputs ended in LookupError and were handled. This is a regression in existing behavior.

get_supported_language_variant() now raises ValueError for over-long codes. Callers fed by untrusted input only catch LookupError. Examples are get_language_from_request() for the language cookie, and get_language_from_path() for a URL prefix such as /xxxx...(600 chars)/ matched by the \w+ regex. A long language cookie or URL prefix with no usable '-' (or with strict=True) will now raise an unhandled ValueError and return a 500 error instead of falling back to the default language.

The cast type comes from `field.db_type()`, which returns pseudo-types such as `serial`, `bigserial` and `smallserial` for AutoField, BigAutoField and SmallAutoField. A bulk_create with explicit primary keys on such a field, or on a FK-less model with an auto pk set, generates `(%s)::serial[]`. PostgreSQL rejects this because `serial` is not a real type. `cast_db_type()` should be used instead, since it maps these fields to real types such as `integer`.

The UNNEST path ignores per-field `get_placeholder()` and any placeholder customisation that the base `assemble_as_sql` applies. Fields with custom placeholders, such as geometry fields or user-defined fields, are cast with a plain `(%s)::type[]` and so lose their wrapping SQL. The eligibility check never excludes such fields, so they get wrong SQL or a wrong result.

The UNNEST path ignores per-field placeholders (`field.get_placeholder`) and special value adapters. It only excludes array db_types and values that have `as_sql`. PostGIS inherits this compiler through the PostgreSQL ops. A bulk_create with 2 or more rows that includes a geometry field would be rewritten to `UNNEST((%s)::geometry(POINT,4326)[])`. The adapted geometry values, such as PostGISAdapter, are put into Python lists and the `ST_GeomFromEWKB` placeholder is dropped. This can fail or insert wrong data. Other fields whose prepared values or placeholders are not plain literals are affected the same way.

_create_alternatives now reads `alternative.content` and `alternative.mimetype`, so it only works with Alternative namedtuples. Existing code that appends plain `(content, mimetype)` tuples to `msg.alternatives`, or assigns a list of plain tuples after construction, used to work and now raises AttributeError when `message()` is called. Only `__init__` and `attach_alternative` convert to the namedtuple. This breaks backward compatibility, even though the new docs say alternatives should only be added through `attach_alternative`.

The check changed from `f.primary_key` to `f in self.model._meta.pk_fields`. With multi-table inheritance, a child model's `pk_fields` is the parent link field, not the parent's `id`. `bulk_update(objs, ['id'])` on a child model is no longer rejected, even though `id` is a primary key field and was rejected before. This is a likely regression for inherited models.

to_python passes self.max_length straight into clean_ipv6_address, which does `len(ip_str) > max_length`. A form GenericIPAddressField created with max_length=None (valid for CharField, meaning no limit) raises TypeError for any value containing ':' instead of validating. `setdefault` keeps the explicit None, so it is not replaced by the default.

If a caller passes max_length=None explicitly (a previously valid way to say "no limit" for a CharField-based field), setdefault leaves it as None. to_python then calls clean_ipv6_address(..., max_length=None), and _ipv6_address_from_str evaluates len(ip_str) > None. This raises TypeError instead of a ValidationError whenever the value contains ':'. Before this change that input worked.

The SelectBox cache guard checks `currentSelect.id` instead of the target `select.id`. If the page loads SelectBox.js and the current select is a plain FK select with no cache entry, the condition is true for every other related select. `SelectBox.add_to_cache(select.id, option)` then runs against selects that may also have no cache entry, such as another plain FK select. That throws a TypeError, because `cache[id]` is undefined, and aborts the update loop. In the opposite case, where the current select is a filter box with a cache entry (the m2m popup path), the guard is false, so other filter-widget selects for the same model never get their cache updated and the new option can vanish on the next redisplay or filter.

The guard checks `SelectBox.cache[currentSelect.id]` but then operates on `select.id`. It should check the cache of the select being updated. If `currentSelect` is a plain select (for example an FK edited or added via popup) and `SelectBox.js` is loaded on the page, the condition is true for every other related select. `SelectBox.add_to_cache(select.id, ...)` then throws a TypeError for any select that has no cache entry, such as another plain FK dropdown. That breaks the update loop. If `currentSelect` does have a cache entry, the branch is skipped and other filter boxes are never added to their cache. The option was also already added via `select.options.add`, so `redisplay` may duplicate or misbehave.

MinimumLengthValidator.get_error_message() applies `% self.min_length` to the ngettext msgids before the translation lookup. The msgids are now "...at least 8 character." instead of the catalog's "...at least %(min_length)d character.", so they no longer match any entry in the locale files. The "too short" error is therefore always shown in English, a regression for every non-English locale. The change also drops `params={"min_length": ...}` from the ValidationError, so code that reads `error.params` loses that data. Custom overrides also cannot use %(min_length)d placeholders, unlike the similarity validator's %(verbose_name)s.

The `%` interpolation is applied to the msgid strings before they are passed to `ngettext()`. The catalog lookup is therefore done on strings like "...at least 8 characters.", which do not match the extracted msgids that contain `%(min_length)d`. The too-short error message is no longer translated for any non-English locale, which is a regression. The `params={'min_length': ...}` was also dropped from the ValidationError, so code that reads `error.params['min_length']` now gets `None`.

The ContentType lookup uses `model__icontains=old_model.lower()` instead of an exact match. Renaming a model such as `User` or `Group` also matches content types like `superuser` or `usergroup` in the same app. The code then rewrites those unrelated models' permission codenames and names to `<prefix>_<newmodel>`, corrupting their permissions or colliding with them. It should filter on `model=old_model.lower()`.

Every permission on the content type is renamed, using `codename.split('_')[0]` as the prefix. Custom permissions are therefore rewritten wrongly. For example, `publish_oldmodel` becomes `publish_newmodel` with a generated name, and a codename like `can_publish_article` becomes `can_newmodel`. Several custom permissions can collapse into one, or conflict with the default ones and be silently skipped by the IntegrityError handler. Only the default add/change/delete/view permissions should be renamed.

The `db` alias is only used for the atomic block. `ContentType.objects` and `Permission.objects` queries, and `permission.save()`, do not use `.using(db)` or `using=db`. When migrating a non-default database, the rename reads and writes whichever database the router picks, usually default, instead of the one being migrated. Permissions may then not be renamed on the target database, or be modified on the wrong one.

The content type lookup uses `model__icontains=old_model.lower()`, which is a substring match. Renaming `Book` to `Novel` also matches the content types for `BookReview` and `Bookmark` in the same app. Their permissions are then rewritten to `add_novel`, `change_novel`, and so on. Those renames either collide and are silently swallowed by the `IntegrityError` handler, or corrupt unrelated permissions. The lookup should be an exact match on `model=old_model.lower()`.

The prefix is taken as `codename.split("_")[0]` and every permission is renamed to `f"{prefix}_{new_model}"`. The name is also overwritten with `Can {prefix} {verbose}`. Custom permissions such as `can_publish_oldmodel` or `publish_oldmodel` get mangled to `can_newmodel` or `publish_newmodel`, with names like 'Can can new model'. Several different custom permissions on one model collapse onto the same codename and conflict. Custom permission names and codenames that don't follow the default pattern are lost. The new name also ignores any custom `verbose_name` the model defines.

The queries ignore the migration's database alias. `ContentType.objects` and `Permission.objects` go through the default router rather than `.using(db)`. Under multi-database setups, `migrate --database=other` reads and saves permissions on the wrong database. The `db` variable is only used for the atomic block.

The permission rename depends on the content type still having the old model name, but ordering is not guaranteed relative to contenttypes' own `RenameContentType` operation. Both pre_migrate handlers insert directly after `RenameModel`. With the default INSTALLED_APPS order (auth before contenttypes), the contenttypes operation is inserted later at the same index and therefore runs first. The content type is then already renamed, so the lookup by the old model name matches nothing and no permissions are renamed. The tests only pass because they list contenttypes first in `available_apps`.

The MRO walk collects every property found in any class's __dict__ and never tracks names that a subclass has already overridden. The old code used inspect.getattr_static, which only looked at the most-derived definition. If a parent defines `foo = property(...)` and a subclass overrides it with a non-property (a model field, a plain attribute or None), `foo` is still reported as a property. `_property_names` is used in Model.__init__ for kwargs handling and in the get_or_create/update_or_create checks, so this can produce wrong results. Examples are a field kwarg being treated as a property setter, or valid defaults being rejected. A `seen` set of names from more-derived classes is needed so only the effective attribute is considered.

The new MRO walk collects every property found in any class's __dict__ and ignores overriding. The old code used getattr_static, which returns only the most-derived attribute. If a parent defines a property and a subclass overrides that name with a non-property (a plain attribute, method, or field), the name is still reported as a property. That misclassifies it in Model.__init__ kwarg handling and in the get_or_create/update_or_create parameter checks. The fix is to track names already seen in more-derived classes and skip them.

Subquery.resolve_expression only catches AttributeError around `self.output_field`. When the query's output field cannot be determined, for example a multi-column `values()` such as `values('tenant_id','id')` used against a composite pk, `BaseExpression.output_field` raises FieldError. That error now escapes at resolve time, even though the old code only resolved the output field lazily when it was needed. A tuple lookup against a multi-column Subquery can therefore crash. The except clause should catch FieldError, or use `_output_field_or_none`.

The comparison `self.output_field != resolved.query.output_field` uses Field equality, which is based on creation_counter and model. An explicitly passed output_field is therefore almost always unequal to the query's own field, even when both have the same type. In that case the resolved query is wrapped in an ExpressionWrapper. The wrapper hides the Query from the right-hand-side introspection that the shim removal was meant to enable, because `isinstance(rhs, Query)` is False. Tuple lookups with an explicit output_field then take the wrong path, and the unsupported-backend check in tuple_lookups.py is skipped. The comparison should be by field type, not instance equality.
